newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Victoria protests Australia asset tax rule changes.
newsitem.headline: Victoria protests Australia asset tax rule changes.

text.p: The Victoria state government on Tuesday criticised the federal government's decision to tighten tax laws on the sale of assets by tax exempt organisations.

The protest follows action on Monday by Australian Treasurer Peter Costello to close a depreciation tax loophole that allowed state governments to structure trade sale of assets to reduce company tax for buyers and lift the sale price of the assets.
Victorian Treasurer, Alan Stockdale said the changes to the depreciation rules for asset sales created different rules for the public and private sectors.
"These changes create an unfair playing field where only purchasers of state assets will be barred from depreciating against market value," Stockdale said in a statement.

Stockdale said the changes would hurt the state's remaining electricity asset sales, including Southern Hydro and the state's electricity transmission grid, PowerNet Victoria, as well as the impending privatisation of Victoria's gas assets.
"The Commonwealth's tax grab will mean a loss of several hundred million dollars for Victorian taxpayers," he said.
Previously, where a tax exempt entity was sold, depreciable assets held within that entity were depreciated for taxation purposes on the basis of their notional writedown value.
These rules could be circumvented by carving out the assets of the entity for separate sale so that the purchaser could claim depreciation on the basis of the purchase price.

Under the new rules, in all sales of depreciable assets by exempt organisations associated with the sale of a business the buyer will get the same opening value for tax depreciation, regardless of how the sale is structured.
Stockdale said all of Australia's states should be concerned about the tax move which he said would threaten economic reforms of inefficient government business enterprises throughout Australia.
The New South Wales government is currently examining the possible privatisation of the state's electricity industry which could raise up to A$22 billion.
